title: Beyond Getting Their Attention
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison reports out from a departmental "Subject Planning & Development Session" at Durrington focused on maintaining, not just securing, student attention. Starting from the school's "All eyes on me in 3, 2, 1" prompt as the mechanism for securing initial attention, Allison compiles the techniques staff identified for keeping it: least invasive intervention (a nod or raised eyebrow rather than a public call-out), explanations punctuated with cold-call questions so students know they could be asked at any moment, deliberate storytelling drawing on Daniel Willingham's research on stories as "psychologically privileged," voice variation and pauses, reducing extraneous cognitive load in slide design, and "Pastore's Perch" -- positioning yourself where you can see the whole room while students work. He closes by tying preparation techniques (I-We-You modelling, "brighten lines" for instructions) into the same attention-maintenance framework.
points: The "least invasive intervention" technique reframes off-task behaviour management as a graduated scale -- a nod or raised eyebrow before a public call-out -- specifically to avoid drawing whole-class attention to one student's lapse.

Cold-calling is positioned as an attention-maintenance tool, not just a questioning technique: if students know an explanation could be interrupted by a question at any point, they have a structural reason to keep listening throughout.

Allison draws on Daniel Willingham's claim that stories are "psychologically privileged" in memory, using Darwin's voyage on the Beagle as a concrete example of embedding narrative structure into an evolution explanation.

"Pastore's Perch" -- positioning yourself in the room (often a side corner, not front-and-centre) so all students are in your field of view during independent work -- is offered as a specific, actionable monitoring technique.
quotes: Students can only learn what they are paying attention to. This prompt gives them a social cue that what the teacher is going to be talking about is important - and so requires their attention.
Rather than drawing attention to this and calling it out in front of the whole class e.g. 'Nick.focus on me now!', take the least invasive intervention.

If students know that your explanation is going to consist of them having to listen to you for five minutes, without any input from them, the reality is, there's no requirement for them to pay attention.

Cognitive scientist Daniel Willingham describes stories as being 'psychologically privileged'. This means our brains are wired to process stories differently and more effectively than other forms of information.
Once you have set students to work on a task, move to a position in the room where all students will be in your field of view.
When it comes to effective teaching, there is very little more important than securing and maintaining attention.
